newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's "Bibi" Netanyahu bounds back from scandal.
newsitem.headline: Israel's "Bibi" Netanyahu bounds back from scandal.

text.p: Bibi's back, with a vengeance.

Bounding off the ropes in hard-hitting television appearances, a beaming Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu came out swinging on Sunday after prosecutors slapped down police recommendations he be charged in a corruption scandal.

Mistakes were made, he said, in the short-lived appointment of a Likud party crony as an attorney general three months ago. But he said the storm over the affair was caused by an Israeli media and opposition that want "to overthrow the government".
Prosecutors, saying their job was to examine legalities rather than political ethics, found insufficient evidence to issue the first indictment against an Israeli prime minister.
"I think he's out of the woods," said political analyst Gerald Steinberg of the Begin-Sadat Centre for Strategic Studies at Bar-Ilan University near Tel Aviv.

"I don't see anybody bolting (from the ruling coalition). Certainly not a party," he told Reuters. "He's overcome a crisis and said this was a political process from the beginning to overturn the verdict of the voters."
Initial signs were good for Netanyahu from within his government of mainly right-wing and religious parties.
Industry and Trade Minister Natan Sharansky said his Yisrael b'Aliya party would hold discussions on how "to ensure that a situation like this does not repeat itself".

But Sharansky, whose largely Russian immigrant party holds seven of the coalition's 66 seats in the 120-member parliament, did not repeat a statement made weeks ago that the government should fall if even 10 percent of the allegations proved true.
The Third Way, another coalition ally, with four seats, also had been widely expected to lead a charge out of the cabinet should Netanyahu be indicted. Israel Radio said it would now stay put.
"I am happy the matter is behind us," said Public Security Minister Avigdor Kahalani, head of the Third Way.

The scandal had overshadowed recent U.S. efforts to revive the Israeli-Palestinian peace crisis which was plunged into crisis when Netanyahu gave the green light for bulldozers to begin building a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.
Steinberg said that while Netanyahu's legal and internal political problems may have eased, the tough issues facing Israel and the PLO had not.

"Terrorism, a Palestinian state, Jerusalem -- those issues haven't changed, but Netanyahu will be able to put more time, effort and thought into looking for ways to advance the peace process," he said.

Netanyahu, in striking out at the opposition, said they would not be able to change his policies on settlements. He also repeated his demand that the Palestinian Authority crack down on terrorism before peace talks could resume.
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat's spokesman Marwan Kanafani called for Israel and the PLO to get back on the peace track, which he said had been held hostage to the scandal.
Former Labour Prime Minister Shimon Peres, who lost last May's general election to Netanyahu, looked crestfallen on hearing the news that his right-wing rival would not be hauled into court.
"The public must hold new elections," Peres told reporters.
Netanyahu pronounced the scandal dead -- "it's finished" -- and dismissed Peres's demand.
"What do you expect him to do? He's the opposition leader. Of course he'll call for new elections," he told CNN.

State prosecutor Edna Arbel said her Justice Ministry team had been divided on the question of indicting Netanyahu. Two legislators from Labour and the left-wing Meretz party said they would appeal to the High Court to order charges be brought.
